claim: No transaction was sent. Over the registered 744-candle series, replaying the deterministic grid plan obtains a lower average buy price than committing the same total quote in one trade at the window's first close, and a lower average buy price than at least half of 1000 seeded random-entry draws committing the same total in the same number of trades at candle closes drawn from the same window.
falsifier: The claim is refuted if the replay's average buy price is not strictly below the buy-and-hold price, or if fewer than half of the 1000 seeded random-entry draws obtain an average buy price above the replay's. It is refuted in a third way that leaves nothing to compare if no buy level fires over the window at all: the record then reports zero triggers and says the comparison is empty, rather than reporting a rate over a denominator of zero. The run record states which of these happened and does not restate the claim as though it had been established.

metric.formula: The plan is docket.agents.grid.plan.build_plan with every input fixed here and none of them read from the series beyond its first observation: reference = the first candle's open in atomic units; lower = reference * 95 // 100; upper = reference * 105 // 100; levels = 11, so the ladder is spaced one percent of the reference apart; size_per_level = 100 * 10**18 (100 USDT); base = WBNB 0xbb4CdB9CBd36B01bD1cBaEBF2De08d9173bc095c; quote = USDT 0x55d398326f99059fF775485246999027B3197955; base_decimals = 18; side_rule = buy_below_sell_above. The replay walks the candles in open-time order and offers each candle's CLOSE, and only its close, to docket.agents.grid.plan.next_action with the set of already-filled level indices; the level it returns, if any, is recorded as a trigger and marked filled. next_action never re-arms a filled level and returns nothing for a price outside the band, so what is counted is first-touch triggers of a one-shot ladder and never a cycling grid; intra-hour highs and lows are not offered, which understates triggers against a venue that would have filled on a wick. A buy fill commits size_per_level of quote and acquires size_per_level * 10**18 // price of base, which is the grid module's own sizing arithmetic, at the level's price exactly. average_buy_price = total_quote_committed * 10**18 // total_base_acquired over the buy triggers, reported as null rather than as a number where no buy level fired. The same quantity is computed for both nulls over the identical window and identical total quote, so the three arms differ in when they bought and in nothing else. random_entry_draws_worse_than_the_replay = |draws whose average buy price is above the replay's| / |draws|, reported as {numerator, denominator, value}. Assumptions, each stated because each moves the number: fills are at the level price with no fee, no slippage and no partial fill, all three of which would raise a real buyer's average price; the series is Binance's BNBUSDT, a centralised venue, while the plan addresses WBNB/USDT on BSC, and the two prices are close but not the same book; and base acquired is floored at each fill, so every arm acquires marginally less base than exact arithmetic would give it.
metric.name: average_buy_price_over_a_replayed_ladder
metric.units: integer atomic units of quote (USDT, 18 decimals) per whole base (WBNB)

null_baselines.name: buy_and_hold
null_baselines.what_it_does: Commits the whole of the quote the replay committed, in one trade, at the first candle's close of the identical window, and holds. Its average buy price is that close. Computed by docket.advantage.v2.replay.buy_and_hold.
null_baselines.why_it_is_the_right_null: It is what the ladder is an alternative to. A grid's entire proposition is that mechanically splitting an entry across levels beats putting the money in at once, so the arm that puts it in at once is the claim's direct opposite and the cheapest thing a caller could do instead. It is also the arm that exposes what a lower average price does not mean: this null is in the market from the first hour and the ladder is not, so the two carry different exposure for the same money, and the base each acquired is reported beside the price each paid.

null_baselines.name: random_entry
null_baselines.what_it_does: Commits the same total quote, in the same number of trades and the same size_per_level, at candle closes drawn uniformly without replacement from the same window: 1000 draws from random.Random(20260811), the seed registered here so the whole distribution can be reproduced exactly. Computed by docket.advantage.v2.replay.random_entry, which reports the distribution of the draws' average buy prices and the share of draws that did worse than the replay.
null_baselines.why_it_is_the_right_null: It is the null that can actually refute the claim. Buy-and-hold differs from the ladder in trade count as well as in timing, so beating it would not separate the rule from the mere act of spreading an entry out. This arm holds the trade count, the size and the window fixed and varies only which moments were chosen, so it isolates the one thing the grid claims: that buying at levels the price fell to beats buying at arbitrary times. If the replay's average price sits in the middle of this distribution, the ladder chose nothing that chance would not have chosen.

question: Replayed over a stated historical series, does the deterministic grid plan's ladder buy at a lower average price than committing the same money once at the start, and than committing it at arbitrary moments in the same window?
stopping_rule: Every candle in the registered series, once, in open-time order. The series is the response body of one keyless HTTPS GET of https://data-api.binance.vision/api/v3/klines?symbol=BNBUSDT&interval=1h&startTime=1782864000000&endTime=1785542399999&limit=1000, stored verbatim: the file IS the response, byte for byte, and the digest above is over those bytes. Binance documents that host as the base endpoint for public market data in its own API documentation (github.com/binance/binance-spot-api-docs, rest-api.md), which is what makes the series first-party rather than an aggregator's copy. The window is closed and entirely in the past, so the same URL returns the same bytes to anybody: the digest is checkable by re-fetching rather than only by trusting this file, and the run record states the result of doing exactly that. What is registered here before the replay is run is every plan input, the trigger rule, both nulls, the random seed and the falsifier. Only the first candle's open is read to build the band, and no later observation was read before this registration was written; the first and last candles were seen while confirming the fetch covered the intended month, which is declared here rather than left for a reader to wonder about.
